content.title: About
content.content: Coconut cake or cupcake is a baked treat made with flour, sugar, eggs and shredded coconut, often enriched with vegetable oil or butter. It has a delicate coconut aroma, a mildly sweet flavor and a moist crumb. Coconut cake works well as a dessert with tea or as a light snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shredded coconut gives the cake its characteristic tropical scent and flavor.
Traditionally coconut cake is baked in small, individual cupcake-sized portions for easy handling.
Coconut cakes are often topped with cream cheese frosting, chocolate drizzle, or extra coconut flakes.
Some recipes replace part of the wheat flour with coconut flour, making the cake lower in carbs.
A gluten‑free version is possible by using a gluten‑free flour blend or by using only coconut flour.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Shredded coconut provides dietary fiber that supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Coconut contains medium‑chain triglycerides (MCTs) that are quickly metabolized for energy.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Coconut cake supplies iron, magnesium and potassium, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: When balanced with coconut, the cake can have a lower glycemic index than a standard vanilla cake.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain flour add B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut flakes or oil.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Coconut cake is relatively high in fats and sugars, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Coconut oil is rich in saturated fat; people with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: If wheat flour is used, the cake is not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy coconut cake as a standalone dessert, slice it and serve with berry sauce, ice cream, or a cup of coffee. It is convenient to pack in a lunch box or as a post‑workout snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer freshness (up to 1 week) keep it refrigerated. Freeze in a sealed bag if you need to keep it for more than a month.

content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin cookie is a soft, aromatic biscuit made with pumpkin puree, warm spices (cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg) and classic dough ingredients: flour, sugar, butter and eggs. Pumpkin gives the cookie a gentle sweet flavor and a bright orange hue.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Pumpkin cookies are traditionally baked in the autumn when pumpkins are abundant at markets.
The combination of cinnamon and ginger with pumpkin is believed to boost mood and create a cozy feeling.
Pumpkin is one of the oldest cultivated plants, grown for more than 7,000 years.

items.title: High in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immune function and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from pumpkin aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: When prepared without added salt, the cookie can be a modest option for sodium‑restricted diets.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6 and folate help maintain energy levels and nervous system health.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: Butter in the recipe supplies essential fatty acids when the cookie is consumed in moderation.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Cookies often contain a notable amount of sugar, which can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Butter and sugar make the cookie energy‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans‑fat risk
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter may introduce trans fats, which should be avoided.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pumpkin cookies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with tea or coffee, used in dessert platters, or crumbled over yogurt, ice cream, or oatmeal for added flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container at room temperature in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator, where they stay fresh for 2–3 weeks. Keep moisture out to prevent the cookies from becoming soft.

content.title: About
content.content: Fresh corn cooked in vegetable oil retains its sweet flavor and crunchy texture. Corn is a worldwide grain crop rich in carbohydrates, fiber, and vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn was first domesticated over 9,000 years ago in Mexico, making it one of the oldest cultivated crops.
There are more than 300 varieties of corn, differing in color, size, and taste.
Cooking in oil enhances aroma and crispness while preserving most nutrients.
Corn is used not only as food but also for biofuel, plastics, and cosmetics.
In the United States, corn occupies over 30 % of all planted acreage, the largest single crop.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: Corn provides a quick source of energy thanks to its high complex carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Corn supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in corn help maintain eye health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Corn provides magnesium, potassium, and iron, essential for muscle and blood health.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to corn.

items.title: Added oil
items.content: Frying adds calories and fat, so consumption should be moderate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, soups, tacos, or served as a side dish. Fried corn is best served hot, lightly seasoned with salt or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fried corn in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, keep it in the refrigerator and consume within a week.

content.title: About
content.content: Pompano (Trachinotus ovatus) is a marine fish from the jack family, native to warm waters of the Indo‑Pacific region. The fillet has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor, firm white flesh and a moderate fat content, making it popular in both restaurants and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pompano is often called the “golden fish” because of its golden‑orange hue.
The species grows quickly, reaching up to 30 cm in length and 1.5 kg in weight within a year.
In Japan, pompano is considered a delicacy and is frequently used in sushi rolls.
Pompano is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are beneficial for heart health.
In the wild, pompano migrates to coastal lagoons for spawning.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help lower cholesterol levels and support cardiovascular function.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Pompano fillet provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, aiding muscle building and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fish contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, essential for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pompano supplies selenium, phosphorus and potassium, supporting immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with larger predatory fish, pompano has lower mercury, making it safe for regular consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including pompano.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the fish has been pre‑marinated or processed, sodium levels can be high.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: As with any raw fish, pompano should be thoroughly cooked to eliminate potential parasites.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pompano fillet can be grilled, baked, steamed, or used in sushi. To keep it tender, cook at a moderate temperature of 180‑200 °C for 12‑15 minutes, depending on thickness. Season with lemon, herbs, olive oil or soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh fillet in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag; the fish retains quality for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen fillet in the refrigerator before cooking.
